History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
37-year-old woman with 2-week history of progressive numbness, tingling, and weakness in the left upper limb (elbow to hand, palmar aspect of 2nd–4th fingers) and a prior transient monocular visual field loss episode; referred urgently to neurology to rule out demyelinating disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis).

History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive numbness and tingling in left arm with subjective weakness.  
• Onset & course: Began ≈2 weeks ago after starting a boxing class; initial mild tingling progressed to persistent numbness and weakness.  
• Distribution: From elbow to hand, palmar side, mainly 2nd–4th digits; occasional shoulder discomfort on movement.  
• Associated features:  
  – Difficulty with fine motor tasks (playing piano).  
  – No pain at rest; no glass-dropping events reported.  
  – One episode of transient left-eye visual field loss (“peripheral vision” deficit) lasting ~20 minutes a few weeks ago.  
  – Intermittent “tired” headaches and general fatigue.  
  – No seizures, loss of consciousness, or lower-limb weakness.  
  – No neck pain (conflicting statement—see Quality Checks).  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Massage, warm baths, ibuprofen—no relief.  
• Review of systems: Denies diplopia, vomiting, gait disturbance, or incontinence.  
• Past recent illness: “Bad cold/flu” one month ago lasting ~2 weeks.

Past Medical History:
• Generally healthy; no chronic conditions documented.  
• Recent upper-respiratory viral illness (resolved).  
• No prior neurological diagnoses.

Medications:
• Ibuprofen – dose/route/frequency not documented (PRN for musculoskeletal pain).  
• Vitamin D – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Iron supplement – dose/route/frequency not documented (infrequent use).  
• Melatonin – dose/route/frequency not documented (PRN for sleep).

Allergies:
• Not documented.

Social History:
• Regular exercise; recently started boxing classes.  
• Plays piano.  
• Alcohol: Social drinker; one recent episode of heavy drinking.  
• Smoking: Not mentioned.  
• Recreational drugs: Not mentioned.  
• Occupation/work schedule: Works long hours (fatigue attributed to workload).

Family History:
• Father: Hypothyroidism; unspecified autoimmune condition.  
• Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia.  
• No known familial neurological disorders.

Physical Examination:
• Not performed/recorded during virtual consult (no vitals provided).

Investigations:
• None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Left upper-limb numbness/weakness with palmar 2nd–4th digit involvement.
  – Assessment: Progressive sensory deficit and weakness; distribution not typical for single peripheral nerve injury; consider central demyelinating process, cervical radiculopathy, or plexopathy.  
  – Plan: Urgent neurology referral for full assessment.

Issue 2: Transient left monocular visual field loss.
  – Assessment: Possible optic neuritis or transient ischemic/vascular event; in context of limb symptoms raises concern for demyelinating disease (e.g., MS).  
  – Plan: Include in neurology referral; anticipate MRI brain/orbits with contrast and visual evoked potentials as guided by neurology.

Issue 3: Possible demyelinating disease (rule-out multiple sclerosis).
  – Assessment: Combination of sensory deficit and visual disturbance is concerning.  
  – Plan:  
    • Urgent neurology appointment.  
    • Likely MRI brain and spinal cord; additional labs as per specialist.  
    • No disease-specific treatment until diagnosis confirmed.  
    • Educated patient on red-flag symptoms (progression to leg weakness, headaches, vomiting, seizures, persistent or worsening visual loss) and advised immediate emergency department attendance if these occur.

General plan items:
• Continue symptomatic ibuprofen if needed for musculoskeletal discomfort.  
• Avoid boxing/exacerbating activities until evaluated.  
• Follow up with GP after neurology visit or sooner if symptoms change.

Quality checks:
• Missing/expected data: Allergies, baseline vitals, formal neurological and musculoskeletal examination findings, medication doses/frequencies, smoking status.  
• Internal conflicts: Patient answered “Yes, absolutely” then “No… nothing” when asked about neck pain (conflict noted).  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional overlaps and minor inaudible segments but main clinical content preserved.
